rag_semantic_descriptions: An automated tool is rapidly attempting to guess FTP credentials by sending repetitive USER and PASS commands to the FTP service on port 21, receiving rejection codes after each failed attempt.
The traffic consists almost entirely of short text-based authentication commands followed by FTP response code 530 (Not logged in), with no actual file transfer operations like LIST, RETR, or STOR.
Each connection to port 21 follows a predictable cycle: login attempt, server rejection, connection teardown, and immediate reconnection — all happening at machine speed.
The packet sizes are distinctly small and uniform because the payloads only contain short username and password strings, unlike normal FTP sessions that would include file transfer data.
Unlike DoS attacks, this brute force shows a relatively balanced ratio of forward to backward packets because the attacker completes the TCP handshake and receives a server response for every guess.
Each individual FTP session has an extremely short duration because the server immediately drops the connection after the failed authentication, and the script instantly starts a new one.
The inter-arrival time between connection attempts is minimal, reflecting automated scripting that fires the next credential pair the instant the previous attempt is rejected.
Deep packet inspection may reveal usernames being tested alphabetically or passwords being pulled sequentially from common dictionary wordlists.
This could be triggered by a broken automated backup script or deployment tool using expired FTP credentials, creating a similar pattern of rapid failed logins.
The attack targets FTP's cleartext authentication mechanism, making it one of the easiest brute force attacks to detect via payload inspection but also one of the most common.
